what_its_for: Atovaquone is used to prevent and treat a serious lung infection called Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP). It is often used in people who cannot take the antibiotic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim). It may also be used to treat or prevent other infections as directed by your doctor.
how_to_take: Take atovaquone by mouth exactly as your doctor tells you. It comes as a liquid suspension — shake the bottle gently before each use. Always take it WITH food, especially a fatty meal (like eggs, toast with butter, or a meal with some fat in it). Taking it with food is very important because food helps your body absorb the medicine much better. Use the measuring spoon or oral syringe that comes with your medicine — do not use a regular kitchen spoon. Swallow the dose and do not mix it with other liquids.
dosing: The usual adult dose depends on what condition is being treated. For prevention of PCP: typically 1,500 mg (10 mL) taken once a day with food. For treatment of PCP: typically 750 mg (5 mL) taken twice a day with food for 21 days. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions, as your dose may be different.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still close to the time you normally take it. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your pharmacist or doctor.
storage: Store atovaquone liquid at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Do not freeze it — freezing will ruin the medicine. Keep the bottle tightly closed and away from direct sunlight and heat. Keep it out of reach of children and pets. Do not use it after the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Do not take atovaquone without food — skipping food greatly reduces how well your body absorbs this medicine. Avoid skipping doses, especially during treatment, as this can allow the infection to come back or get worse. Tell your doctor about all other medicines you take, because some medicines — like rifampin, rifabutin, and metoclopramide — can make atovaquone less effective. Avoid taking it with antacids without checking with your pharmacist first.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: a severe skin rash, hives, or blistering skin; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; trouble breathing; severe nausea, vomiting, or stomach pain; yellowing of your skin or eyes (signs of liver problems); extreme tiredness or weakness; dark-colored urine; or signs that your infection is not getting better or is getting worse. Also contact your doctor if you develop any new or unusual symptoms while taking this medicine.
when_it_works: For treatment of PCP, you may start to feel better within the first week, but it is very important to finish the full 21-day course even if you feel better sooner. For prevention, atovaquone works as long as you keep taking it as directed. Do not stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel well.
special_populations: Elderly patients: Use with caution; your doctor will monitor you closely. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor before taking this medicine if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, as the risks and benefits need to be discussed. Breastfeeding: It is not known if atovaquone passes into breast milk; talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: Dosing in children is based on weight and age; follow your doctor's instructions carefully. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as your dose or monitoring may need to be adjusted. HIV-positive patients: This medicine is commonly used in people with HIV/AIDS; follow all additional care instructions from your doctor.
